newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia rice growers lobby against PNG duty.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia rice growers lobby against PNG duty.

text.p: Australian rice growers began lobbying the Papua New Guinea government on Wednesday to reverse its decision to slap an 11 percent import duty on rice and said initial talks were productive.

The Rice Growers Cooperative said it was caught by complete surprise by the move, which was announced on Tuesday in an austere mini-budget unveiled in Papua New Guinea, one of the Australian rice-growing industry's top export markets.
Australia exports about 100,000 tonnes of paddy rice to its developing northerly neighbour each year, or about 10 percent of total annual production, the cooperative said.

The cooperative denied the import duty would have a major impact on Australian rice exports to Papua New Guinea and said rice growers here recently overcame a steep devaluation of the Papua New Guinea currency, which increased the cost of imports.
Asked what the impact was likely to be, cooperative general manager Jim Kennedy told Reuters: "I wish I knew.
"It's certainly the case that when the country devalued its currency between 25 and 30 percent (two years ago), there was an increase in cost and a decline in consumption," he said.
"But in some ways rice is a strange commodity because it's the last one a hungry person cuts off his list."
But, Kennedy added, "There's no way I can dress this up as a positive development."
The cooperative held what it called "productive" discussions on the import duty with Papua New Guinea officials on Wednesday.
"They are prepared to talk about it," Kennedy said.

Papua New Guinea Finance Minister Chris Haiveta said in his budget speech to parliament in Port Moresby that the new duty would raise 11 million kina (US$8.4 million) in calendar 1997, its first full year of operation.

Outlining the government's fiscal agenda for 1997, Haiveta also announced rises in personal income and corporate tax rates, and rises in excise duties on diesel fuel, gasoline, cigarettes, tobacco, beer, liquor and wine.
He also deferred planned cuts to import tariffs on raw materials such as chemicals, fertiliser, steel, aluminium and capital equipment machinery.

The revenue measures, designed to keep the overall budget deficit at one percent of grodd domestic product, come against the backdrop of a possible breakdown in relations between the Papua New Guinea government and the World Bank, which is coordinating a US$345 million loans-for-reform programme.
The aid donors, which have so far paid out US$200 million, are withholding the second tranche until it is satisfied Port Moresby has met all conditions attached to the funds.
